articles.title: Wicker and the rise of the ‘monster romance’: why audiences are falling for the non-human
articles.author: Natalie Wall, PhD Candidate in English Literature, University of Liverpool
paras: Wicker is an unorthodox love story from husband-and-wife filmmaking team Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson. Based on Ursula Wills-Jones’s short story, The Wicker Husband, it blends satirical folk fable with elements of the modern rom-com.

The film, set vaguely in the middle ages, follows a lonely fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) who commissions a husband made from wicker (Alexander Skarsgård). Ultimately she falls in love with her handmade companion.

Colman’s fisherwoman is pitied for her unmarried status which is believed, at least in part, to stem from her perpetual fishy stench, prompting ridicule from the villagers. However, set against the comically bad marriages of those around her, she doesn’t seem to be in such a bad position, highlighting that, under patriarchy, women are damned if they do and damned if they don’t.

The addition of a preternaturally devoted wicker husband to the village creates a new benchmark for marriage – one that stirs and intrigues the women and profoundly worries the men. It’s a bawdy yet astute exploration of what it means to challenge the heterosexual status quo.

Wicker arrives amid a remarkable boom in stories centred around relationships between the human and non-human. Monsters, aliens, dragons, demons and even household objects have increasingly moved from the margins of fantasy culture into the centre of popular romantic storytelling.

Films such as Lisa Frankenstein and A Useful Ghost have recently attracted smaller cult fan followings. And earlier successes including The Shape of Water, Warm Bodies and Edward Scissorhands have helped establish the idea that unconventional romantic partners can carry emotionally resonant mainstream narratives.
What has changed is not simply audience tolerance for the strange. Instead, our cultural ideas about intimacy, desire and romance are being reimagined.

Stories of humans forming relationships with beings they’ve made or transformed appear throughout mythology and folklore. Perhaps the most well-known example is the Greek myth of Pygmalion, in which a sculptor falls in love with Galatea, a statue of a beautiful woman that is brought to life.

There are countless other examples: stories appear in Jewish legends about beings made of clay called golems; northern European folktales tell of the selkies which can shapeshift between seal and human forms by removing or putting on their seal skins. And a whole multitude of fairytales hinge on magical transformations. Such narratives ask enduring questions about what makes someone human, what constitutes life and whether love can overcome radical physical differences.

Wicker’s romantic hero is clearly part of this long genealogy of made, crafted or transformed partners. But the character, while not necessarily or strictly monstrous, also speaks to the rising interest in “monster romance” within the rapidly expanding romance and romantasy book market.
Romantasy has become one of the publishing industry’s most successful genres and within it, readers have enthusiastically embraced relationships that cross species boundaries.

Katee Robert’s bestselling The Dragon’s Bride follows a relationship between a woman and a dragon-like being and Ruby Dixon’s wildly popular Ice Planet Barbarians series has crafted an entire romantic saga between various women and aliens from a frozen planet.

Monster romance fans have carved out their own niche on platforms like Instagram and, perhaps most significantly, TikTok’s BookTok, where they passionately champion their favourite books, couples and monster romance tropes.

Many of these books originated outside traditional publishing. Lauren Roberts’ Powerless and Jennifer L. Armentrout’s A Soul Of Ash And Blood were propelled by reader-driven recommendation networks and algorithmic infrastructure.

Communities like BookTok helped self-published authors build dedicated audiences long before major publishers recognised the commercial potential of the trend. As a result, stories once regarded as too strange or specialised for mainstream audiences are now bestsellers and the cultural appetite for the unusual has grown.

The popularity of monster romance has prompted critics to ask why readers are increasingly drawn to non-human partners. One explanation is that these narratives create distance from familiar romantic conventions.

By removing relationships from recognisable social realities, writers gain space to explore intimacy in new ways. Monster romances often challenge assumptions about things like beauty and gender expectations. The central conflict is rarely whether the monster is worthy of love; in fact, the stories frequently present the non-human figure as unusually attentive, loyal and emotionally available.

This dynamic has led some critics to connect the popularity of monster romance to “heteropessimism”: a growing cultural sense that conventional heterosexual relationships feel disappointing, unequal or exhausted.

Rather than abandoning romance altogether, audiences may be searching for alternative ways of imagining sexuality and emotional fulfilment. Here the monster becomes a vehicle for exploring possibilities outside of the patriarchal heterosexual partnership. (However, it must be noted that many of these romances are still broadly heterosexual, despite their play with gender roles and expression.)

But Wicker doesn’t just feature a non-human lover; he’s also a man-made one. Within our climate of heteropessimism and dating despair, stories about creating our ideal partner feel even more relevant. They examine the relationship between creation and desire, as well as asking what happens when people attempt to manufacture intimacy rather than discover it.

Digital technologies increasingly mediate romantic relationships. Dating apps encourage people to sort through seemingly endless options of potential partners while profiting from users’ desire for connection. And AI chat bots have introduced new discussions about the nature of companionship and the potential for relationships with digital beings.

Against this backdrop, the wicker husband embodies contemporary anxieties about loneliness and connection while also offering a fantasy of uncomplicated and unwavering devotion. The film emerges from a cultural landscape already primed for stories about loving the strange, the constructed and the non-human.

articles.title: Political information increasingly comes from pop culture, outside of partisan silos but where male creators – and sometimes misogyny – dominate
articles.author: Karrin Vasby Anderson, Professor of Communication Studies, Colorado State University
paras: Research on political polarization points to how people’s preferred news outlets and social media use create information silos, environments in which people primarily encounter views consistent with their own, further cementing those views.
But this research often omits an important source of political information: popular culture, from influencers and podcasts to comedy, television and movies.

Politics are intertwined with popular entertainment media. The current president is a former reality television star who was reelected in 2024 with the help of comedy podcasters like Joe Rogan. Blockbuster films such as “The Odyssey” spark controversy and turn into political footballs, while late-night talk show hosts must skirt the Trump administration’s regulatory ire with their politically oriented humor.

While we know a lot about the news-consumption habits of Republicans and Democrats, there is less data about the other places that people encounter political ideas. This is particularly true for younger people, who are increasingly likely to get political content from social media influencers and popular culture sources.

Political consultant Sarah Longwell of The Bulwark recently told The New York Times’ Ezra Klein that many people in her focus groups get political information from an “algorithm-driven information environment” populated by influencers, comedians and sports personalities. She noted that the “overlap between politics and culture” creates a “vibe” that shapes many people’s political decision-making.

As co-founders and research affiliates of Colorado State University’s Center for Democracy, Art, and Popular Culture, we conducted a survey that documents the pop culture preferences of Americans ages 18-49.

We wanted to know whether the siloing that has been observed in Americans’ news environments is replicated when younger Americans are consuming entertainment media that often contains political content.

That matters, because popular influencers and entertainers who cross partisan boundaries have an increased ability to shape the political “vibe” discussed by Longwell. And an important finding from our survey is that many of the favorite creators and outlets ranked in the survey feature men and promote masculinity.
Favorite influencers and podcasts
Pop culture is the diverse collection of cultural productions consumed by members of a society: films, television series, video games, art, music, comedy and the like.
We asked 741 Americans to name their top influencers, podcasts, comedians, musicians, video games, films and television series. We examined results by age and political party.

Respondents first identified which pop culture outlets they engaged with and then shared their favorites in each content category. The answers were diffuse, but trends are evident in the top three listed by people across political affiliations.
Both the Democratic and Republican parties have turned to influencers to reach voters – particularly young voters – who “don’t consume traditional political news.”

In our survey’s lists of favorite influencers, three creators who rose to fame staging viral stunts, interviewing celebrities and playing video games on YouTube and the live streaming platform Twitch dominated the list: MrBeast was No. 1 for Democrats, Republicans and independents. Republicans and independents ranked Kai Cenat in their top three, while IShowSpeed was No. 2 for Democrats and Republicans.

A similar pattern of the same names populating each list is evident in people’s favorite podcasts. “The Joe Rogan Experience” and “Call Her Daddy” were in all groups’ top three, while Republicans and independents also ranked the “Tucker Carlson Show” and “This Past Weekend with Theo Von.”

Joe Rogan and Theo Von are comedians turned podcasters, whereas Tucker Carlson rose to fame as a right-wing pundit. “Call Her Daddy” is an outlier on our list insofar as it is hosted by a woman, Alex Cooper, and is known for frank discussions of sex and relationships.

The website Campaigns & Elections reported that in 2024 half of all registered voters surveyed who listened to at least one podcast per month said that podcasts had some influence on their vote. The site reported that in the 2024 presidential election, those podcast listeners favored conservatives.

Our survey helps to explain why. Rogan, popular with all three groups, has long voiced libertarian ideas and platformed right-wing politicians. Von occupies a similar space, and Carlson is conservative. Both are favorites not just of Republicans but also independents.
Favorite comedians and video games
Political scientists and media scholars have demonstrated how comedy can influence politics. Our survey found considerable overlap among political partisans’ favorite comedians.

Dave Chappelle, creator of the boundary-breaking Comedy Central series “Chappelle’s Show,” topped the list for Democrats and Republicans and was the second favorite of independents. Bill Burr, known for comedy that is both cocky and aggrieved, was in the top three for Republicans and Democrats, while Shane Gillis, whose comedy The New York Times says “fits into the evolving meaning of conservatism,” was second and third for independents and Republicans.

Video games are another shared pop culture venue where Americans of different political affiliations are encountering one another as they play, via discussions with other players on Twitch and by participating in the comments sections of gameplay livestreams.

Researchers have demonstrated that young people, in particular, are exposed to diverse political views when engaging with one another in “online participatory activities that are non-political in nature.”

For example, one study examined how a viral trend of “building Trump’s wall” while playing Fortnite spurred political discussions both inside the game and in comments on gameplay videos and social media posts.

U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez demonstrated the political power of the medium in 2020 when she livestreamed herself playing the game Among Us, an online, multiplayer deduction game similar to the popular party games Mafia and Werewolf. Ocasio-Cortez playing the game with U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar and prominent gamers was billed as a get-out-the-vote effort and earned 4.5 million views.
In our survey of video games favored by people of different political affiliations, Call of Duty, Fortnite and Sims appeared on all three lists.
Our data suggests that these pop culture spaces are thus not partisan silos. But that doesn’t mean they are free of particular ideologies.

Some of the most popular creators – Rogan, Von, Carlson and Gillis – appeal to, or helped construct, the manosphere, a loose collection of online communities that promote masculinity and often reflect misogynistic attitudes.
Burr’s comedy is not politically conservative. But The New York Times said that it “gives voice to the aggrieved confusion of the white heterosexual guy adrift.”

Chappelle is known for his satirical critiques of racism. But in his more recent Netflix stand-up specials, he voiced anti-trans sentiments that Mother Jones called “indistinguishable from, and grist for, the material of conservative streamers and right-wing edgelords.”

Our survey did not ask respondents why they preferred these influencers, podcasts, comedians and video games. Academic research has shown that pop culture audiences don’t passively accept every message a creator delivers. Nevertheless, the dominance of male creators and the prevalence of misogyny and transphobia in their humor and commentary is significant.

Whether convened online or in person, the groups that gather via popular culture do not fit into the partisan silos that have formed around news and social media outlets. That makes the gendered nature of these lists even more significant, because the manosphere vibes are not relegated to one side of the political spectrum.

articles.title: The Black designers redefining British fashion by drawing on their own heritage, culture and history
articles.author: Andrew Ibi, Programme Leader BA Fashion: Design & Communication, School of Art and Creative Industries, Liverpool John Moores University
paras: British fashion has always been shaped by creative exchange: forged inside melting pots, authored by radical style communities – and often fuelled by class and migration.

Over the past decade, we’ve witnessed the distinct emergence of a new genre centred on the Black British experience. It has seen its designers drawing on their unique histories, the most prominent of which are Martine Rose, Priya Ahluwalia, Nicholas Daley, Bianca Saunders, Saul Nash and Grace Wales Bonner, with the latter appointed to lead Hermès menswear in 2025.
The story is evolving. A new wave of talent is developing its own visual languages, challenging notions of Britishness and the expectation of what Black fashion design should look like.
At London Fashion Week in September 2026, Francesca Lake presented Wake the Town, a spectacular exploration of Jamaican funeral traditions, nuanced dress forms and their cultural contradictions.

Lake is developing an immersive design language that celebrates cultural memory and contemporary invention. The Jamaican-born, London-based designer is skilfully disrupting historical style notes to subvert ruffled lace crinolines and elaborate church headwear while purposing theatrical silhouettes into a distorted proposal of British identity.

Joshua Ewusie, founder of E.W.USIE, is busy transforming everyday cultural references into luxurious and sophisticated fashion. His In Lieu of Flowers, spring/summer 2027 collection, draws on the domestic interiors of Ghanaian households, using contemporary and traditional crafts as a cultural bridge.

Rising fashion star Tolu Coker is reimagining British tailoring through fusing her Nigerian heritage and her working-class upbringing in west London. Her February 2026 London Fashion Week presentation, which was attended by King Charles, took direct inspiration from the council estate where she grew up. The king’s presence was a significant moment of recognition for cultural value and Coker’s contribution to luxury fashion.

Elsewhere, debuting labels like are flourishing. NUB contemplates the convergence of heritage and metropolitan London life, while GOYAGOMA, founded by Traiceline Pratt, approaches womenswear through exploring identity, femininity and the everyday experiences of diasporic communities.

Storytelling and cultural reportage have themselves become a form of luxury. But this “luxury” is no longer just about expensive fabrics or high-end logos – instead, the real desirability and prestige come from the meaningful stories, history and authentic cultural heritage woven into the clothes.

At a time when immigration and national identity remain contested political questions, the work of these designers consolidates a vivid picture of modern Britain, shaped by overlapping cultures, communities and histories. Crucially, it offers a more expansive account of identity than political categories often allow.
Beyond a single Black aesthetic
History, experience and heritage remain central to storytelling. But designers are equally keen to debate how Black bodies should be dressed and understood.
More established voices like Bianca Saunders have already reworked traditional menswear silhouettes, challenging uncomfortable and familiar ideas about gender.

Saul Nash, also a choreographer and dancer, has assimilated technical sportswear with movement, helping to stage new expectations of masculinity – shaping a genderless, softer, fluid outcome. Nigerian-British designer Mowalola has been using a provocative design vocabulary to explore sexuality and popular culture with her distinctive use of leather, challenging gender expectations and respectable dress codes.

Jamaican-born and Cayman Islands-raised Jawara Alleyne’s experimental garments challenge commonplace notions of Black male bodies and masculinity. Through draping, slashing, knotting and pinning, his assembled propositions offer a unique culture clash of Caribbean traditions and London’s punk histories. Like many of his contemporaries, Alleyne’s education was completed at Central Saint Martins.

A 2019 graduate of University of the Arts London’s College of fashion, Abigail Ajobi uses luxury streetwear to engage with social issues, community empowerment and youth culture, intrinsically challenging the role of fashion and the runway.
A generation shaping Britain’s style future

Perhaps the most significant evolution is freedom to fearlessly author, build and create personal artistic worlds. Yaku Stapleton’s fantastical collections draw on family storytelling and creative character building influenced by video games. The designer imagines immersive environments which spawn playful, experimental clothing.

Torishéju Dumi also transforms her tailoring through experimental construction, drawing on historical references and unconventional silhouettes. Her work reflects on her personal cultural heritage, but she does not position it as its central purpose.

Ethiopian-born, London-based Feben approaches fashion through a surrealist lens, citing “form and matter” as merging contributors to distinctive textured and draped forms. Ronan McKenzie’s label, Selasi, works with the simple notion that women should “understand and listen to their own bodies” – and her cultural identity is embedded in the process.

In 2023, I co-curated The Missing Thread at Somerset House in London, an exhibition that recovered overlooked contributions to British fashion. One was Joe Casely-Hayford’s, which was shaped partly through responses to political and societal changes; at the same time, he defined the first iteration of Black British identity in fashion.

Today, this new generation is writing the next chapter while expanding into unexpected directions. Their work excels amid political tensions and arguments about immigration and belonging, but they are not necessarily presenting overt political statements. Being Black, or British, has never been a monolithic experience.

Culture is not fixed – it is a continuously altered by its participants. It is a tapestry to be refined, deconstructed and repurposed for its own users. These trailblazing young designers bring a huge range of voices to British fashion, expanding its cultural imagination and redefining who has the authority to construct and create identity.

articles.title: How London’s 1838 ‘great stink’ created the modern vampire
articles.author: Rae Gillibrand, Lecturer, Premodern History, University of Leeds
paras: Long before modern medicine could name the invisible terrors ravaging Victorian Britain, the public found a face for contagion: the vampire.

A new exhibition at the University of Leeds’s Treasures of the Brotherton Gallery, Quite Shameless: Cultural Reflections on the Vampire, explores how this supernatural predator became a stand-in for the period’s deepest anxieties about disease, contagion and contaminated air. The exhibition brings together manuscripts, books, prints, medical objects and theatrical materials, including items from the Bram Stoker collection.

Throughout the 19th century, rapid industrialisation brought huge numbers of people into British cities, where poverty, overcrowding and fragile infrastructure triggered devastating outbreaks of disease. As such, people were deeply concerned with questions of health and sanitation. However, knowledge of germ theory was not fully established until the end of the century and, in the meantime, people believed disease was spread by bad smells known as “miasma”.

In the summer of 1838, London experienced a heatwave that resulted in the “great stink”. The Thames was heavily polluted with rotting food, human waste and corpses of humans and animals. As temperatures soared, the river levels fell, leaving its contents to bake in the sun. The resulting cholera and typhoid epidemics were attributed to the terrible smell coming from the river, rather than the contaminated water supply.

These fears inspired John Leech’s illustration Silent Highwayman, published in Punch magazine in 1858 and on display in the exhibition. The cartoon presents a grim reaper like skeleton rowing through the bodies of dead animals in the shallow waters of the Thames. The caption, “your money or your life” demands that the government invest in public sanitation or risk losing more lives to disease.

Just as Leech presents disease through the personification of death, Bram Stoker did so through the character of the vampire. In his novel Dracula (1897), the titular vampire’s chambers contain a heavy miasma that is described by protagonist Jonathan Harker as “composed of all the ills of mortality and with the pungent, acrid smell of blood”.
However, bad smells weren’t the only explanation behind the spread of disease in the late-19th and early-20th centuries. People were also quick to blame migrants, travellers and foreigners.

An example of this in the exhibition can be seen in John Tenniel’s illustration, “Back!”. Published in Punch during the cholera outbreak of 1892, the drawing personifies cholera as a spectral figure attempting to enter Britain on a ship from abroad. Britannia holds out her hand, refusing entry to the migrant cholera, to prevent the spread of the disease into the country.
The cholera outbreaks of the 19th-century were a source of fear for their contemporaries. Over the course of the century, it is estimated that the disease killed about 140,000 people in the UK.

Stoker grew up in the shadow of this fear. His mother, Charlotte Thornley Stoker, had witnessed a devastating cholera outbreak as a teenager in her hometown of Sligo, Ireland. In just six weeks, about 640 local people had died. The blame fell on travellers who were believed to have brought the disease into the town. In her memoir, Thornley Stoker recounted the horrific treatment of one of these travellers:
One I vividly remember, a poor traveller was taken ill on the roadside […] [the people of Sligo] dug a pit and with long poles pushed him living into it and covered him up alive.

These stories of migrants targeted by fearful communities were formative for the young Bram Stoker and likely influenced his writing. Like his mother’s experiences with Cholera, Stoker’s villain Dracula is a traveller who enters a country at a port town, bringing a deadly and inexplicable disease with him. And, just like the cholera epidemics of the 1800s, the “disease” of vampirism is fought against by medical doctors. Most notably, in the case of Dracula, the Dutch medical doctor Abraham van Helsing and his former student Dr John Seward.
The representation of vampires as both migrants and bringers of disease becomes even more explicit in F.W. Murnau’s 1922 silent movie, Nosferatu.

In the film, Count Orlock (Max Schreck) travels from Transylvania to Germany on a ship infested with rats, bringing with him an unspecified disease known as “the great death”. While cholera was not spread by rats, the association between rats and disease was strong in the early-19th century mindset. The character design for Orlock is especially rodent-like, with elongated fangs resembling a rat’s prominent incisors.

For people in the 19th century, the vampire provided a way to make invisible threats visible. By transforming the transmission of disease into a literal monster, vampires make an intangible fear tangible and perhaps most importantly, into something that can be confronted.
Quite Shameless: Cultural Reflections on the Vampire is at the University of Leeds’ Treasures of the Brotherton Gallery. Tickets are free and the exhibition will run until May 29 2027.

articles.title: Horace Walpole’s The Castle of Otranto turned architecture into horror’s greatest weapon
articles.author: Peter Nelson Lindfield, Lecturer in Architectural History, Cardiff University
paras: What does a haunted castle look like? Perhaps you imagine a ramshackle or imposing structure with towers, pinnacles and undefined spaces hidden in the shadows; some of its “prickly” gothic details picked out by moonlight. Threateningly ill-defined buildings, enough for our imagination to fill in the gaps, seem to be the ideal catalyst to spark terror.

Ever since the publication of Horace Walpole’s The Castle of Otranto on Christmas Eve 1764, the novel has inspired visions of dark corridors, towering staircases, subterranean passages and moonlit chapels. The first novel to be identified as “gothic”, it’s presented as an ancient tale translated by the fictional William Marshal of Ghent.

Otranto cemented many of the themes that came to define the gothic literary genre: supernatural apparitions, family curses, ancient prophecies and mystery. Even so, one of the novel’s greatest achievements lies in an obscure character hidden in plain sight: the castle itself.
Woven throughout Otranto’s pages is a remarkable, changing architectural setting playing host to the novel’s action. The building, however, remains elusive.

You cannot draw a map of the castle because it is not mapped out in sufficient detail. This is despite Walpole, in the guise of Marshal, teasing readers in his preface to the first edition that it is “undoubtedly laid in some real castle”. He writes:

The author seems frequently, without design, to describe particular parts. The chamber, says he, on the right-hand; the door on the left-hand; the distance from the chapel to Conrad’s apartment: These and other passages are strong presumptions that the author had some certain building in his eye.

Perhaps it describes Walpole’s very own romantically styled gothic “castle”, really a country villa, in well-to-do Twickenham. Built across decades from 1749, Strawberry Hill recreated the architecture and sense of history found in Britain’s medieval cathedrals and homes. Strawberry Hill did not provide Otranto’s specific details. Instead, it helped shape the castle’s atmosphere: its dark passages, stained glass and carefully orchestrated contrasts of light and shadow embody what Walpole called “gloomth”.

This effect is certainly echoed in the novel’s castle setting, yet Otranto is not Strawberry Hill in disguise as often suggested. The novel’s architecture is stranger, less fixed and far more elusive than any real building.

Readers encounter Otranto’s architecture by degrees. Walpole never provides a complete description of the building nor its exact appearance. Instead, the castle emerges in fragments, glimpsed through moments of fear, wonder and supernatural disruption.
By refusing to pin down Otranto’s appearance and complete geography, Walpole encouraged generations of readers, artists and architects to imagine the castle for themselves.

Many drawings and paintings illustrating Otranto’s scenes were produced by fans of the novel. Those Walpole celebrated the most were produced in 1796, more than 30 years after the novel’s first publication, by teenage artist Bertie Greatheed Jr. Pasted into his personal copy of Otranto and today housed at Yale University’s Lewis Walpole Library in Connecticut, Walpole considered these watercolours the finest illustrations of his gothic story. He praised their ability to capture emotions and supernatural effects. On February 22 1796, Walpole wrote to the artist’s father.

I have seen many drawings and prints made from my idle […] not one of them approached to any one of your son’s four – a clear proof of which is, that not one of the rest satisfied the author’s ideas – It is as strictly, and upon my honour, true, that your son’s conception of some of the passions has improved them, and added more expression than I myself had formed in my own mind; for example, in the figure of the ghost in the chapel, to whose hollow sockets your son has given an air of reproachful anger, and to the whole turn of his person, dignity.

Beyond the figures’ deep psychological intensity, what makes these drawings so compelling is Greatheed’s use of tangible architectural settings. Rather than serving as passive gothic backdrops, the spaces actively drive the drama. Pointed arches frame terror and underline monstrous acts, vast interiors dwarf the figures and deep shadows hint at hidden dangers. By grounding the supernatural in believable, relatable architecture, Greatheed amplifies the emotional impact of each scene.

This relationship between architecture and fear lies at the heart of gothic fiction. Walpole believed medieval architecture possessed a unique capacity to stimulate the imagination. Gothic buildings, with their dramatic contrasts of light and dark, their hidden corners and soaring spaces, encouraged emotional responses that more orderly classical architecture rarely inspired. They could evoke awe, wonder, melancholy and terror.

Each Halloween, gothic architecture returns to popular culture in the form of haunted houses, castles, abbeys and ruins. Yet Walpole’s Castle of Otranto reminds us that the most unsettling gothic buildings are often those we cannot fully see. Like Greatheed’s illustrations, they leave enough hidden in shadow for the imagination to complete the picture.

articles.title: Pan’s Labyrinth at 20: a powerful, symbolic tribute to Spanish resilience in the face of fascism
articles.author: Keith McDonald, Associate Professor. Film Studies and Media, York St John University
paras: This autumn marks the 20th anniversary of Pan’s Labyrinth, Guillermo del Toro’s elaborate and deeply sorrowful film about a young girl caught between two dangerous worlds in rural Spain in 1944. The film is back in cinemas to celebrate the anniversary.

The film tells the story of Ofelia (Ivana Baquero), who finds herself shifting between the “real” above-ground world half a decade after the end of the Spanish civil war, and an underground “fantasy” realm where ancient forces recognise her as a lost princess.

It is a perennially relevant tale of tyrannical power and those who rebel against it. Highly lauded on its release, the film’s stature has grown in the last two decades. It appears in prestigious international polls of the greatest films of the 21st century, and many view it as the pinnacle of del Toro’s body of work to date.

One reason the film resonates with audiences and critics alike is its compelling, dense visual language. This abundance of symbolic images draws on del Toro’s impressive capacity to use grandiose mythic signs infused with pop-cultural emblems.
The iconic Pale Man (Doug Jones), for example, is an amalgam of Francisco Goya’s Saturn Devouring His Son and a poster for Don Coscarelli’s 1979 horror film Phantasm.

Ofelia’s liminal existence is reflected through contrasting visuals. We see her placed in the hands of her stepfather, the despotic Falangist Captain Vidal (Sergi López), draped in the bland greyness of militarism, and watch as she is mesmerised by the mysterious Faun (also played by Doug Jones), who blends with this bizarre and beautiful underworld.

Ofelia, who speaks rarely during the film, aptly, defying the subservience the verbose Vidal demands. Instead, she reads and responds to the world through visual symbols that give meaning to the horrific ongoing violence of Franco’s regime above ground, and the tempting-yet-terrifying netherworld below.

The Faun gives Ofelia a seemingly empty book that magically fills with images and text as her quests continue. In the film’s logic, the power of creation and alchemical image-making gives her a sense of self, direction and purpose in the labyrinthine environment.
Cinema’s resilience under censorship

Censorship, and the rebellious ways art can respond to it through potent symbolism, are central to the film. In 1938, the Comisión Nacional de Cinematografía was added to Spain’s already harsh legislative controls over film exhibition. This added film fiction as a category to be controlled alongside newsreels and documentaries, tacitly recognising cinema as a provocative art form.

Film-makers were both required and well equipped to use the suggestive power of symbolism, deeply embedded in Hispanic culture and heritage (evident in the visual language of pictorial art, religion and folklore) to address the trauma of the civil war and life under Franco.

For example, in Carlos Saura’s 1966 The Hunt, three middle-aged civil war veterans reunite to lead a small hunting party searching for rabbits in the location where they once trapped and shot down loyalists. Their nostalgic hunting trip and fond reminiscences turn to bitterness and eventually violence against one another, suggesting that the horrors of their past have caught up with them in implicit, rather than explicit terms.

In Pan’s Labyrinth, the most horrific actions take place not in the mysterious underworld, full of monsters, mysteries and terrors, but in the real world above, where Captain Vidal wreaks the bizarre blend of maniacal violence and controlled intent that is the festering hallmark of fascism.

A tragic scene sees a father and son interrogated after they have been found with a gun. They swear that the father has been hunting rabbits to feed their family. Vidal brutally batters the son to death with a bottle and shoots the father in the throat before casually searching through his satchel only to find several rabbits, which makes no difference whatsoever to him.

Pan’s Labyrinth also incorporates magical-realist films made under censorious conditions. The most prominent of these is Víctor Erice’s 1973 The Spirit of the Beehive. Set in a Castilian village in 1940, the film follows Ana (Ana Torrent), a young girl whose life is transformed after James Whale’s 1931 adaptation of Frankenstein comes through town via a mobile cinema.

Captivated by the film’s power, Ana’s reality shifts, and she helps a wounded Republican soldier, seeing his plight as mirroring that of the abandoned creature. The film’s tribute to the power of cinema and symbolism has had a deeply formative effect on del Toro and, of course, influenced his recently fulfilled dream of adapting his own version of Frankenstein in 2025.

Del Toro has stated that he is “not a filmmaker who can speak directly about politics without addressing it through fable or parable. It’s just not in my make-up.” Pan’s Labyrinth can be seen not only as a film that draws on a vast pantheon of symbolically coded imagery, but also as one that pays homage to cinema’s resilience under censorship, confirming the indefatigability of the human imagination.
Keith McDonald works for York St John University

articles.title: Pan’s Labyrinth at 20: how Guillermo del Toro created his timeless dark fairy tale
articles.author: Daniel O'Brien, Lecturer, Department of Literature Film and Theatre Studies, University of Essex
paras: Fantasy accounts for only about 28 minutes of Pan’s Labyrinth’s 119-minute running time, yet these supernatural scenes are what many viewers remember most about Guillermo del Toro’s 2006 film. Now back in cinemas to mark its 20th anniversary, a rewatch makes it easy to see why.
Despite everything del Toro has achieved since, including his Oscar success for The Shape of Water (2017), Pan’s Labyrinth remains for many (including me) his magnum opus.

The film weaves together the brutality of a war drama with a dark, mythic undercurrent. Set in 1944, five years after the Spanish civil war, the story follows General Francisco Franco’s regime as it brutally suppresses lingering Republican resistance. The grim reality is filtered entirely through the eyes of a child, Ofelia (portrayed by Ivana Baquero).

Described this way, it is difficult not to think of the Upside Down world in Stranger Things (2016-25). Particularly given the striking visual similarities between the Demogorgon and del Toro’s iconic Pale Man (played by Doug Jones, who also plays the Faun and has appeared in six of the director’s films).

In a recent rewatch of Pan’s Labyrinth, I was reminded of the film-maker’s expertise and the dark beauty I had remembered so vividly back in 2006. What I hadn’t remembered, however, was just how sparse the overtly supernatural elements are, occupying less than half an hour of the total run time. Their relative scarcity confirms just how powerful and arresting del Toro’s imagery is, and how less can be more when expertly applied.

The monstrous Pale Man, for example, an anthropomorphic beast with eyes in the palms of his hands who gorges on children, occupies surprisingly little screen time. Yet it came to dominate my memory of the film. Publicity stills probably had something to do with that – but the lasting trauma the Pale Man represents is also testament to del Toro’s skilful layering of two parallel worlds.
The fairytale world mirrors the horrors of Francoist Spain during the summer of 1944, predominantly experienced through the eyes of 11-year-old Ofelia.

The nightmarish Pale Man finds a real-world echo in Ofelia’s military stepfather, Captain Vidal (Sergi López). He’s an authoritarian narcissist and avatar of Francoist power. Vidal is dedicated to hunting down the Spanish maquis (anti-Francoist guerrilla fighters) and subjecting them to horrific cruelty. He exerts a different but no less suffocating form of control over Ofelia and her pregnant mother. He regards her unborn baby less as a child than as an heir, destined to continue his name and legacy.

This theme of legacy extends into the film’s mythical realm when the Faun reveals Ofelia’s true identity as a lost princess. To reclaim her throne, she must complete three quests that directly mirror the horrors of her everyday world. In one trial, Ofelia retrieves a key from the belly of a giant toad – a task that runs in parallel with the maquis rebels’ desperate bid to steal Vidal’s storeroom key for food and supplies.
A maze of cinematic influences
The film echoes Jim Henson’s Labyrinth (1986), which turns 40 this year. As in Henson’s film, Ofelia’s journey into a mysterious world becomes a test of growth, doubt and temptation.

Ofelia’s quest to heal her mother and save her brother recalls Sarah’s mission in Labyrinth. Other moments echo classic 1980s dark fantasy. A chalk portal brings Tim Burton’s practical effects in Beetlejuice (1988) to mind. Meanwhile, the final chase through the maze evokes Stanley Kubrick’s The Shining (1980).

Yet del Toro has been careful to distinguish his labyrinth from other mazes. In an interview around the film’s original release, he observed that “a maze is a place where you get lost”, whereas “a labyrinth is essentially a place of transit”. This distinction is key to appreciating del Toro’s complex vision. The film is rich because it charts a transitional moment for Spanish society, while Ofelia’s journey embodies hope, agency and choice against a backdrop of fascism, which del Toro described as an “institutional lack of choice”.

Choice, obedience and temptation come vividly to the fore in the iconic Pale Man sequence. Warned by the Faun not to eat anything from the creature’s table, Ofelia, like Eve, succumbs to temptation and chooses to eat two grapes from its banquet. This moment of choice, along with many others, also evokes del Toro’s complex relationship with religion.

Raised Catholic but later describing himself as “lapsed”, the influence of religion reveals itself throughout del Toro’s work and in many of his artistic choices. For example, the imagery of a young girl and a faun in Pan’s Labyrinth may bring C.S. Lewis’s The Chronicles of Narnia (1950) to mind, yet del Toro had already declined the opportunity to direct 2005’s The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, in part because he was uncomfortable with the explicit Christian resurrection of Aslan

In Pan’s Labyrinth, religious symbolism is instead appropriated into something altogether murkier, becoming entangled with ambiguous structures of power. The wounds in the Pale Man’s palms evoke the stigmata, while Ofelia’s temptation by the forbidden feast recalls the forbidden fruit and subsequent expulsion from Eden.

Yet neither offers a straightforward Christian allegory. Del Toro instead twists familiar religious ideas into something strange and unsettling, intertwining them with structures of power, while allowing his child protagonist to question obedience.

Del Toro’s uncompromising vision ultimately meant waiving his director’s salary to get the film made as he wanted rather than sacrifice his artistic choices. Twenty years on, Pan’s Labyrinth remains every bit as rich, unsettling and powerful as I remember it feeling in the cinema.

articles.title: Pittsburgh’s ‘Green Man’ was a real person – why the legend outlives the facts
articles.author: Jeffrey Tolbert, Associate Professor of American Studies and Folklore, Penn State
paras: Every semester I teach a class called History of Monsters, Aliens and the Supernatural at Penn State. It fills up quickly, because students, like many people, are fascinated by the supernatural.
During the course, students occasionally bring up the western Pennsylvania tradition of the “Green Man.”
As a folklorist, I study the traditions people practice and share in everyday life, from jokes and family recipes to birthday customs and ghost stories.
The story of the Green Man shows how legends and history can tangle – and how each person who retells a legend helps remake it.
What makes a legend a legend

In everyday speech, “legend” often means a story that isn’t true. For folklorists, a legend is a story about something that may have happened in the real world, told as if it could be true but always open to debate.

As Linda Dégh, a prominent Hungarian American folklorist, once put it, “The legend is a legend once it entertains debate about belief. … The sounding of contrary opinions is what makes a legend a legend.”
This is in contrast to myths, for example, which are sacred creation or explanatory stories set before or outside of normal time.

Importantly, myths and legends are not simply false narratives. They contain different kinds of truth, which depend on the perspectives of the people sharing them. Folklorists don’t study such stories in order to disprove them. Our goal is to understand why these stories matter to people.

Legends are distinct from history because they do not center on established, generally agreed-upon facts about past events. They are more like contested historical narratives that may at times align with consensus history and at other times subvert it.
The real man behind the Green Man

According to news coverage, the man at the center of this legend, Raymond Robinson, was 8 years old in 1919 when he climbed a bridge near Beaver Falls, in Beaver County, Pennsylvania, to reach a bird’s nest and touched a live electrical line. He survived, but lost his eyes, nose and part of an arm.

Robinson lived with his family in nearby Koppel. To avoid attention, as the legend goes, he took to walking along a quiet stretch of Route 351 at night. Some called him “Charlie No-Face,” but “Green Man” seems to have caught on among people from farther away.
A number of people claimed to have met and spoken with him directly during his nighttime walks. Some who met him were kind to him, news outlets reported; others, less so. Robinson died in 1985.

A reporter from the Post-Gazette suggests that the truly frightening part of the story is how Robinson became an object of fear and ridicule. In a KDKA report, Robinson’s great-niece describes him as an exceptionally kind person. And PennLive reporter Claudia Dimuro writes, “But maybe in between seeking these thrills from supposed ghosts lurking in abandoned tunnels, we should stop and wonder whether they were once someone real.”

The “thrills” Dimuro refers to stem from a practice folklorists call legend-tripping – that is, deliberately visiting a location associated with a legend, often in order to experience some part of the legend for oneself.

These articles note that many people deliberately set out to visit Robinson while he lived and went on his nighttime walks. While it might be tempting to assume that an encounter with a real human being would end the supernatural legend of the Green Man, these real-life encounters may have actually bolstered the legend.
Legend, truth, fiction, fact

Popular media coverage of folklore often tries to debunk it. The Discovery Channel show “MythBusters” was built around testing popular beliefs, such as whether a penny dropped from the Empire State Building could kill someone. Many news articles about the Green Man also engage in debunking by highlighting the real life of the man behind the legend. That urge makes sense, especially when false claims can hurt real people. Casting Robinson as a monster dehumanizes a man who lived with severe disabilities, and his family still lives with that legacy.

Legends occupy an unstable place between fiction and reality. Robinson was real, and so were his nighttime walks. But the Green Man of legend – a glowing, threatening figure with supernatural powers who supposedly lived in a tunnel – was not. The so-called Green Man Tunnel in South Park Township seems to have had nothing to do with Robinson’s actual life.
Still, people “really” met the “real” Green Man, and those meetings, for better or for worse, contributed to the legend. Instead of laying it to rest, those encounters likely helped preserve it.

I doubt that debunking the supernatural or monstrous parts of the Green Man legend will make it fade away. Still, I’m sympathetic to the desire to honor the real man at the heart of the story, and to push back on the dehumanization and ableism that drew such interest to his story in the first place. And the link between the monstrous legend and Robinson’s real life is itself a historical matter. Robinson was a real person who really became the central figure of a legend. To fully tell his history means acknowledging that legend as part of it.

Legends are, after all, talk about a supposed past. As a form of talk, legends persist as long as we continue talking about them. But legends are by definition debatable, their claims are never solid, and they’re never really on stable ground.

If, in the future, students bring up the Green Man in my Monsters class, I’ll acknowledge that, yes, this is an example of a legend. It features a man made into a kind of monster. I’ll note that legends, as talk about things that may have happened and people who may have been, are never neutral.

But I’ll also suggest that, because legends are debatable, unstable and contested, there’s always room for us to challenge and correct problematic claims when we hear them, and to bring humanity to stories unjustly focused on monstrosity. We can, if we choose to, tell a different version of the story.

articles.title: AI may quickly generate ideas, but working with people leads to more creative ones
articles.author: Clin Lai, Postdoctoral Fellow in Artificial Intelligence and Society, Brandeis University
paras: The productivity gains of generative AI are often touted as the main reason for its rapid adoption. Much like how a calculator can instantly solve mathematical equations too long for the human brain to compute, generative AI can help someone quickly summarize long articles and draft emails.
But beyond productivity, a key question remains: How is AI affecting quintessentially human activities, such as collaboration and creativity?
As cognitive scientists who study creativity, we recently conducted an experiment that explored how working with AI – rather than humans – affects originality and other aspects of creativity.
Speedy and wordy doesn’t mean creative

Creativity is often tied to what cognitive scientists call “divergent thinking.” One way of measuring divergent thinking is to ask someone to come up with a range of uses for a common item, such as a brick or a book. This is known as the alternate uses task.
Researchers then compare the number of ideas and the originality of these ideas to assess creative capacity.

Large language models appear to have the “number of ideas” part down pat: They can generate many more ideas than humans can. This ability to produce more – and produce that high volume more quickly – partially explains why more than half of new articles online are now generated by AI.

These texts, however, are often verbose, with redundant information. Researchers who tested 12 AI chatbots across different companies on thousands of factual questions found that their answers were often many times longer than human-written answers, with the actual answer making up only about 42% of the text. The rest was largely extra padding: repetitive information, unnecessary background details and explanations that went into too much detail or veered off topic.
Large language models also seem to struggle with the originality of their outputs.
An ‘original’ idea – again and again

In our research, we compared the results of people working on the alternate uses task with another person to those who collaborated with ChatGPT on the same task. We randomly assigned 208 participants to work with either AI or another person.

We found that compared with two people taking turns together, people working with ChatGPT wrote longer responses on the alternate uses task. But human pairs came up with more creative ideas than the humans working with ChatGPT.

We also found that the ideas people came up with when working with other people tended to be more distinct and diverse than those who worked with large language models. Individual AI suggestions could be quite creative – using a book as a sound dampener, for example – but ChatGPT presented that same idea across many separate sessions, making its overall pool of ideas more homogeneous.

Other studies have highlighted the homogeneity of generative AI’s outputs. One group of researchers found that using AI repeatedly over time to generate images often results in bland, generic pictures – what they call “visual elevator music.” Other studies have found that although AI may help an individual write a more creative story when compared with their preexisting work, AI-assisted writing as a whole, across all users, tends to be more similar.

All of this makes sense when you think about how large language models work. After being trained on massive sets of texts, large language models predict the next most likely words. Because their training processes were similar, different large language models, whether it’s ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, tend to have similar cadences, diction, syntax and suggestions – particularly when compared with the work of two random human writers.
In other words, generative AI’s ideas may seem unique in a vacuum. But if everyone’s using AI, the ideas and writing style start to converge.
Creative collaboration is a long game
Finally, we also found that the creativity benefits of working with another person became even stronger as the collaboration progressed.

Ideas can be measured through semantic distance, which is a way of quantifying how distinct individual concepts are. Over time, interacting with other humans seems to result in larger semantic distance than interacting with a chatbot. In other words, people may traverse more creative terrain when collaborating with other people. Meanwhile, the tendency for ideas to converge in chatbot-assisted brainstorming could accumulate, potentially narrowing the range of ideas people explore over the course of a long period of time.
This is important because many creative projects involve long-term engagement.

For example, to launch a new product, researchers have found that it takes an average of 27 months to go from the initial idea to the finished product. More innovative products can take as long as 54 months.
Chat-human before you ChatGPT
If you want to work with a chatbot, how can you preserve your creativity in the face of AI’s tendency toward homogeneity?

Some research suggests using what’s called “persona prompting.” Like talking to other people with different perspectives, users could provide an extensive prompt to give chatbots a pretend personality that can simulate different types of people. For example, you might prompt it to respond as if it is “a male college professor from India who is an expert in teaching” or “a 58-year-old female founder of a construction company.” Researchers found that while this persona prompting increased ChatGPT’s idea diversity, the overall range of ideas still fell short of that produced by human writers. These findings echo other recent research suggesting that chatbots are poor simulators of human personality.

If you need help with a creative task, we suggest going back to the basics: Chat with a person before chatting with AI. They’ll have idiosyncratic personal experiences that can’t be captured by a large language model that’s trained to generate average responses.

Composing a sentence, however modest, is a creative act, whether it’s in a text to a friend or a wedding speech. As AI is integrated into workflows, it’s important to remember that other people can still be a valuable resource. Work completed in collaboration with other humans feels more meaningful.
They might not respond as quickly or as comprehensively. But chances are they’ll have something more interesting to say.

articles.title: Five ways to find your personal style outside of trends and algorithms
articles.author: Rose Davison, Senior Lecturer in Fashion Marketing, Management and Communication, Nottingham Trent University
paras: Fashion is currently trapped in a hyper-accelerated trend loop. Every week there’s a new “core” or “maxxing” style to contend with – such as balletcore or whimsymaxxing. They zoom in and out of our cultural consciousness with alarming speed.

These fads are so numerous that we can be confounded with choice, so oddly specific that we need a new wardrobe to be part of them, and so rapid that there is rarely time to understand or assimilate our own style preferences.

In 1937 the author, critic and art historian James Laver developed Laver’s law, charting how clothing styles evolve in public perception over a 160-year cycle. He asserted that clothing was seen as “charming” after 70 years, but “ridiculous” after just 20.

Yet today, 1990s and Y2K fashion dominate consumer trends. At first glance, this speed-run of recent history appears to clash with the weekly conveyor belt of TikTok micro-trends. In reality, they are two sides of the same algorithmic phenomenon.

Rather than cycling through distinct eras sequentially as Laver predicted, social media feeds flatten time entirely. Decades of vintage subcultures and instant micro-aesthetics are collapsed into the same endless scroll, allowing a 1990s minimalist silhouette to coexist alongside a week-old “whimsymaxxing” viral trend.
Having lived through both the 1990s and Y2K style moments the first time around, it is clear they are also defying Laver’s timeline – they remain far from “ridiculous” to younger generations.

No one’s 20s and 30s look the same. You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps, or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone.
Social media hasn’t killed personal style, it’s killed how we communicate it
A brief history of embroidery – and how to get started yourself
Indie sleaze: a brief fashion history, from messy rebellion to mainstream revival

In Fashion: A Philosophy (2004), the Norwegian philosopher Lars Svendsen described how the “traditional replacement logic of fashion […] has itself been replaced by a logic of supplementation”. Rather than a style coming in and going out of vogue, we now continuously accumulate more styles – produced and consumed faster than ever before.

This shift is driven not only by the speed of online micro-trends, but by mass accessibility and algorithmic marketing. If you feel overwhelmed by the choice and density of the clothing that is around us, that’s probably because at no other time have we been surrounded by so much stuff and had so many possibilities marketed at us. As psychologist Barry Schwartz examines in his book The Paradox of Choice (2016), an overabundance of choice – whether on high street shelves or digital feeds – ultimately causes demoralisation rather than liberation.

Consider the barrage of styles that have recently dominated social feeds. Whether it is the viral “mob wife” or “brat” aesthetics or the heralded return of “indie sleaze”, consumers are inundated with manufactured novelty.

These “must-haves” do not emerge to fill genuine human need. Does the environment truly require us to “whimsymaxx” our way to the nearest landfill? This rapid turnover exploits our impulses – provoking a knee-jerk reaction to buy new goods to avoid feeling outdated.

Paradoxically, recent trends such as normcore, dadcore and gorpcore seem to revel in an “anti-style” aesthetic – prioritising utility and nonchalance over a fashion statement. Yet even these styles require consumer participation. Technical gear designed for extreme outdoor survival from heritage performance brands like Arc'teryx and Gore-Tex is repackaged as high-fashion streetwear, attached to considerable price tags, and pushed through the exact same hyper-accelerated promotional machinery.
Developing an authentic personal style amid this constant marketing can feel daunting. But there are ways to turn down the noise and reclaim your sartorial agency.

Look to figures whose attitude and expression transcend trends – whether it is the uncompromising tailoring worn by Lauren Bacall, the unabashed classicism of Paul Newman or the eclecticism of contemporary stylist Catherine Baba.

Looking back to past eras – before commercial algorithms and fast-fashion feeds dictated daily wear – reveals how individuals curated distinct personal styles. They relied on craftsmanship, silhouette and their personal eccentricities, rather than algorithmic prompts.
2. Reevaluate where, when and what you buy

It sounds daft, but only buy things you actually like. It’s difficult to not enjoy getting dressed when you are choosing from garments that you bought because they make you happy. Go into charity shops and vintage shops and see what you are drawn to in a space where there is (slightly) less trend interference.
3. Think about your messaging
Consider what your wardrobe communicates about your character. Are those puffed sleeved, smocked, tiered dresses really a match for a steely personality, for example?
Evaluate whether transient high-street silhouettes align with your actual lifestyle and self-image, or if they merely reflect passing promotional campaigns.

Look to personal or family archives – photographs of parents, grandparents or historical eras – to identify timeless silhouettes and durable materials that offer a real alternative to influencer-driven fast fashion. If your mum looked great in a ribbed polo neck, there’s a strong chance you will too.
Clever styling, repairing, dyeing and managing your wardrobe can help you to see that what you have is probably enough.

The commercial landscape we live in always tells us we need the latest this and the newest that but, as Schwartz examines in The Paradox of Choice, having the extravagance of choice present in shops and online, actually does us harm.
Breaking away from the feeds, the reels, the ads and the algorithm will mean you can curate a less dictated sense of style – and have a wardrobe that truly speaks to who you are.

articles.title: Primetime: in this taut morally complex thriller, ambition, entertainment and justice collide
articles.author: Laura O'Flanagan, PhD Candidate, School of English, Dublin City University
paras: Director Lance Oppenheim creates a grim and grubby world in Primetime, steeped in the sweat and compromised ambitions of its characters. But below the film’s grimy surface is a sharp examination of the personal and professional concessions people make in pursuit of success.

Inspired by real events, Primetime follows American television presenter Chris Hansen (Robert Pattinson), whose NBC reality TV series To Catch a Predator became a ratings sensation between 2004 and 2007.

The film is set in 2006 as Hansen, working with producer Andie Bender (Merritt Wever), oversees sting operations. In the set-up, men are lured into houses believing they are meeting underage children, only to be confronted by Hansen and his cameras.

Among those recruited is aspiring actor Dan Plum (Skyler Gisondo) as TV bait, whose involvement offers another perspective on the enterprise. Pattinson’s performance as Hansen carefully reveals the deep insecurity beneath his relentless ambition. Constantly comparing himself with more successful figures, Hansen is consumed by a desire for fame and recognition.

At times Pattinson appears almost reptilian, observing those around him with a cold, calculating intensity. Hanson’s commitment to exposing wrongdoing becomes increasingly difficult to separate from his determination to make a name for himself. There is something distinctly predatory about his pursuit of success, troubling the neat division between predator and prey on which To Catch a Predator depends.

Wever is excellent as the harried Bender, whose commitment to the project and qualms about its ethics seem curiously dependent on its success. She treads the line between the pressures of keeping the programme afloat and the ease with which moral reservations give way to professional ambition.

Gisondo is impressive as “Decoy Dan”, bringing a tightly controlled earnestness to an aspiring actor who sees the sting operations as a career opportunity. His vulnerability during the first encounter also exposes reality TV’s potential to cause harm.

Oppenheim’s background in documentary filmmaking informs Primetime’s visual approach. The security footage and VHS-style imagery lend the film a rough authenticity which evokes the television of the mid 2000s.

Period details, such as popular drama Lost as a ratings rival, reinforce this sense of time and place. And the curious appearance of former NBC executive Jeff Zucker as himself, among a cast of actors portraying real-life figures, further blurs the distinction between fiction and documentary.

The surveillance footage also places viewers in the uncomfortable position of watching the sting operations unfold, making us participants in the spectacle of exposure. To Catch a Predator effectively appointed itself judge and jury, voyeuristically subjecting suspected sexual predators to public humiliation in the name of protecting children.

Oppenheim explores the uneasy morality of an enterprise whose targets draw hatred and anger even as its methods invite scrutiny. By drawing us into these encounters, he raises questions about our own responsibility as viewers. We are, after all, consuming the very entertainment whose ethics the film calls into question.

It has been a remarkable year for Oppenheim, whose Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything, co-directed with Nathan Fielder, has become an unlikely US box-office hit. The film took more than $45 million (£34m) in its first ten days. Both films suggest a fascination with controversial public figures and the uncomfortable questions surrounding their pursuit of success.

In Primetime, this produces a seedy, unsettling portrait of ambition, anchored by excellent performances and a distinctive visual approach. Its interest in the people behind the cameras extends to those watching, implicating the audience in the spectacle it depicts.
The film leaves us to consider how easily the pursuit of justice can become a form of exploitation, and what responsibility we bear for the entertainment we consume.

articles.title: Medieval ghost stories featured rotten flesh, the walking dead and spoon-stealing spirits
articles.author: Alex Brown, Associate Professor of Medieval History, Durham University
paras: Stories of wandering spirits and the restless dead were common in the Middle Ages. These ghostly encounters were recorded in a wide variety of medieval literature.

Medieval ghost stories combined folklore traditions with religious doctrine. The widespread belief in purgatory – a place where souls were cleansed of sin before entering heaven – helped fuel the belief in ghosts.

Spirits of the departed were thought able to return, exhorting the living to pray for them and make amends on their behalf to aid their passage through purgatory. As a result, medieval ghost stories often contained a strong moral and religious message.

Historians have long been fascinated by a series of 12 ghost stories written down in the early years of the 15th century at Byland Abbey, a Cistercian monastery in north Yorkshire. They recorded a bizarre and eclectic array of ghosts, featuring shape-shifting spirits, miracle stories and the walking dead, who crept up on the living.

These tales were clearly intended to scare people. They referred to the “terrors of the night” and to spirits rising from their graves to “disturb and terrify villagers”. One graphically described a woman sinking her hand into a spirit’s flesh as if it were rotten and insubstantial.

Some of those who encountered these spirits were even said to have been hurt or fallen “ill and languished for many days” afterwards. Yet the primary aim of most of the ghosts was not to physically harm the living. In one story, a spirit threw a man over a hedge but then caught him on the other side so he did not get hurt. Instead, ghosts most often sought the help of the living.

In one of the stories, two men were walking in a field when suddenly one fled “in great terror” as the other man was “left struggling with a spirit who badly tore his clothes”. The man managed to “conjure” the ghost – a vital step enabling the living and dead to communicate. The ghost then confessed that he had been excommunicated for stealing silver spoons. He begged the man to restore the spoons and request absolution on his behalf, which he duly did.

Such stories were intended to be instructive. The reader was encouraged to think about others who might be in purgatory, and to pray for their salvation. They were also exhorted to consider their own behaviour and to amend their ways before their own demise.

Some of the stories made this explicit. In one which revolved around a real inheritance dispute, the sister of Adam de London, a minor landowner in Ampleforth, was compelled to wander the village after her death. She explicitly threatened her brother that if he did not restore the disputed property to her husband and sons, he would suffer the same fate as her upon his death.

Some of these moral messages are timeless, but others clearly conveyed the concerns of medieval landowners. In one story, a poor spirit was being “grievously punished” because he had not ploughed his master’s land sufficiently well.

Religious faith was vital in confronting such spectral visitors. In one story, a man named William de Bradeforth was followed by a ghost crying “how, how, how”. William commanded the spirit to depart “in the name of the Lord and by the power of the blood of Jesus Christ”. The ghost was said to flee, “looking like a piece of canvas unfurling its four corners and billowing away”.

In another, a spirit appeared to a tailor called “Snowball” in various forms, including a raven and a dog. The spirit admitted that he only had the power to visit the man because he had not heard Mass that day.

Sometimes the moral instruction in such stories was less clear. For example, the revenant of James Tankerlay, a former rector, came forth and blinded his former concubine. No one sought to communicate with him or put him to rest. Instead, they opted for banishing the ghost by digging up his corpse and throwing his remains into a mire.
This echoes earlier stories of revenants and the walking dead. In this tradition, the return of the dead could be prevented by beheading, burning or otherwise mutilating the bodies of the deceased.

Archaeological evidence suggests this may not have been just a literary invention but was occasionally carried out. Skeletons from between the 11th and 13th centuries at the deserted medieval village of Wharram Percy in north Yorkshire had a series of post-mortem mutilations that may have reflected such anxieties around the walking dead.
Living an upright life might have promised peace in heaven, but when it came to keeping the dead in their graves, medieval communities clearly preferred not to take any chances.
Alex Brown is currently the Principal Investigator of a Leverhulme Trust funded project on 'Modelling the Black Death'.

articles.title: Hailed as a 21st-century Greek masterpiece, Gjak retains its bloody power in English translation
articles.author: Gonda Van Steen, Koraes Chair of Modern Greek and Byzantine History, Language and Literature, King's College London
paras: Blood is the word. Blood in every sense. Gjak: Tales of Blood, written by Dimosthenis Papamarkos, was a massive success on publication in 2014. It won the prestigious Academy of Athens award and has become one of the most widely discussed works of 21st-century Greek literature.
Now it has found its perfect voice in English in the 2026 translation by Siân Valvis, a British-Greek literary translator working across Greek, Russian, French and Portuguese.

With her translation of Gjak, Valvis has now also successfully navigated the language and ethos of the Arvanite villages. The Arvanites are a bilingual group, descendants of migrants from Albania in the 13th to 16th centuries who settled in central and southern Greece. Their language, Arvanitic, is an Albanian dialect seasoned with loans from other languages and dialects.
Gjak was written in a dialect blending elements of Arvanitic into Greek. Valvis’s English translation is startling: a vivid, at times raw, at times highly lyrical text.

As an expert in the trauma of 20th-century Greek warfare, the weight of cultural memory and the complex historical identity of the Arvanite people, seldom have I read a work that exudes so much linguistic and cultural ruggedness and sensitivity all at once. I came away with a sense of uneasy familiarity and I am sure you will too, for there is no place to hide from the bloodlines and trails that link us all.

Gjak is series of interconnected short stories, which strive to portray what ordinary life was like remote villages that had become more Greek as they were formalised as part of the Greek nation state. Each explores what it was like living in the aftermath of the Greco-Turkish wars of 1919 to 1922.

With Greek and Arvanite soldiers returning to their villages, peace – internal as well as external – should have had a real chance at being restored. No such thing. These warriors carry blood and guilt with them and these infiltrate deeply into blood lines, family and fraternal bonds, love and homoerotic relationships, village and community dynamics, even relations across borders and oceans (to reach the diaspora communities of the New World).

Blood and the guilt associated with death become the proverbial red threads tying Papamarkos’s short stories together. These connected bloody threads are also revealed in the ballad-style poem that functions as an intermezzo at the book’s midway point. This ballad is not an interlude of lightness. It is, rather, the lyric tale of a courageous woman’s encounter with bloodthirsty Death himself. With this ballad, too, the female voice appears loud and strong in the text and in the translation. Women are subjects in most of the stories otherwise, strong though they may be – and certainly no strangers to blood and violence.

Valvis’s translation does these bloody threads justice at every turn. The work here pushes at the boundaries of literature, linguistics, history and nationalism. But even more so, the translator has unflinchingly portrayed PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder). Papamarkos does not hold back when describing how victims of PTSD behave, with continued violence that can turn very visceral, and Valvis has managed to translate this vividly and sensitively.

Thankfully, the translator carefully explains in a note what is at stake, what choices she has made and what the trajectory of the translation has been (a five-year-long process for a book of about 140 pages).

Valvis’s unsettlingly direct language succeeds in having the readers question themselves. Can we write off violence and revenge as belonging to others or are we complicit too? The character aptly called the “knocker” explains, in Valvis’s deliberately ironic (misspelled) language and grammar:

Folk don’t mind foulness so long as it stays out of sight and it’s not their hands getting dirty. So long as they can go out, dressed up, arm in arm wi their lady friends, free of stink, and pick up cutlery with hands that aren’t swollen with blood and tuck into their steak without getting dirty. That’s what it means to be sivilized. Stepping on shit in high heels. It’s hidden, the work I do at Union, just like what I did in the war was hidden.

Valvis’s translation enjoys the endorsement of Papamarkos, who received the prestigious Academy of Athens award for Gjak. This English translation is the rightful winner of the Elizabeth Constantinides Translation Prize, given out by the Modern Greek Studies Association of North America. I fully expect that more accolades will follow for a translation so rich and so bold. Papamarkos’s stories have been adapted for the stage many times, and I anticipate that Gjak in translation will see successful production runs as well.
